claim: Ribosome biogenesis is a complex and energy-demanding process requiring tight coordination of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and ribosomal protein (RP) production.
source: Ribosome biogenesis is a complex and energy-demanding process requiring tight coordination of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and ribosomal protein (RP) production.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about ribosome biogenesis.

claim: Rapidly growing yeast cells produce about 2000 ribosomes per minute.
source: This massive biosynthetic program permits rapidly growing yeast cells to produce about 2000 ribosomes per minute (Warner, 1999), which is critical for sustaining high rates of growth (mass accumulation) and proliferation.
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner, 1999.

claim: Ribosome assembly requires the coordinated and large-scale assembly of four rRNAs with 79 different RPs.
source: At the same time, though, ribosome assembly poses a constant threat to cellular protein homeostasis and continued growth, since it requires the coordinated and large-scale assembly of four rRNAs with 79 different RPs, the latter of which are known to be highly prone to aggregation (David et al., 2010; Pillet et al., 2017; Rand and Grant, 2006; Weids et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations about RP aggregation.

claim: Ribosomal proteins are highly prone to aggregation.
source: the latter of which are known to be highly prone to aggregation (David et al., 2010; Pillet et al., 2017; Rand and Grant, 2006; Weids et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Unassembled RPs in metazoans activate p53 through titration of its negative regulator MDM2.
source: Indeed, unassembled RPs in metazoans have long been known to activate p53, through titration of its negative regulator MDM2, and conserved p53-independent pathways that respond to perturbations in ribosome assembly are now beginning to emerge (James et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to James et al., 2014.

claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae lacks p53.
source: Given the absence of p53 in yeasts, Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a promising model system in which to uncover ancestral processes that might monitor ribosome assembly to regulate growth and protein homeostasis in eukaryotes.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast genetics.

claim: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is a central actor in Protein Quality Control (PQC) and protein homeostasis (proteostasis) in eukaryotes.
source: Heat shock factor 1 (Hsf1) is a central actor in Protein Quality Control (PQC) and protein homeostasis (proteostasis) in eukaryotes, in both stressed and unstressed cell, and in pathological situations (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: Hsf1 is a direct modulator of tumorigenesis.
source: Notably, Hsf1 is a direct modulator of tumorigenesis and becomes essential, as it is in budding yeast (Solís et al., 2016), to support growth of malignant cells (Santagata et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Solís et al., 2016 and Santagata et al., 2013.

claim: Hsf1 is essential in budding yeast.
source: Notably, Hsf1 is a direct modulator of tumorigenesis and becomes essential, as it is in budding yeast (Solís et al., 2016), to support growth of malignant cells (Santagata et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Solís et al., 2016.

claim: Hsf1 prevents protein aggregation and proteome imbalance by driving the expression of a small regulon including genes encoding essential chaperones (Hsp70/Hsp90), nuclear/cytoplasmic aggregases, and proteasome components.
source: Hsf1 prevents protein aggregation and proteome imbalance by driving the expression of a small regulon including genes encoding essential chaperones (Hsp70/Hsp90), nuclear/cytoplasmic aggregases, and proteasome components (Solís et al., 2016; Mahat et al., 2016; Pincus et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Ribosome Quality Control complex (RQC) is conserved from yeast to human.
source: Interestingly, studies in budding yeast reveal that the Ribosome Quality Control complex (RQC), conserved from yeast to human (Brandman et al., 2012), increases Hsf1 activity under conditions of translation stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: The RQC increases Hsf1 activity under conditions of translation stress.
source: Interestingly, studies in budding yeast reveal that the Ribosome Quality Control complex (RQC), conserved from yeast to human (Brandman et al., 2012), increases Hsf1 activity under conditions of translation stress.
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: A conserved PQC mechanism referred to as Excess Ribosomal Protein Quality Control (ERISQ) specifically recognizes unassembled RPs in the nucleus and targets them for proteasome degradation.
source: Recently, a conserved PQC mechanism referred to as Excess Ribosomal Protein Quality Control (ERISQ) was described that specifically recognizes unassembled RPs in the nucleus and targets them for proteasome degradation (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b), thus illuminating observations made 40 years ago showing that excess RPs are rapidly degraded (Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Warner, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: Excess RPs are rapidly degraded.
source: thus illuminating observations made 40 years ago showing that excess RPs are rapidly degraded (Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Warner, 1977).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Warner, 1977.

claim: The ubiquitin ligase Tom1 plays an important role in ESRIQ by preventing the accumulation of detergent-insoluble RPs.
source: Sung and colleagues showed that the ubiquitin ligase Tom1 plays an important role in ESRIQ by preventing the accumulation of detergent-insoluble RPs.
evidence: Refers to work by Sung and colleagues, implicitly citing their publications.

claim: A decrease of ribosome abundance protects cells against proteotoxic stress.
source: Given the tremendous investment of cellular resources involved in ribosome production (Warner, 1999) and the fact that a decrease of ribosome abundance protects cells against proteotoxic stress (Guerra-Moreno et al., 2015; Mills and Green, 2017), it might be expected that cells have evolved mechanisms to rapidly decrease RP gene transcription in the face of defects in ribosome assembly, in order to both save energy and reestablish cellular proteostasis.
evidence: Supported by citations to Guerra-Moreno et al., 2015; Mills and Green, 2017.

claim: RP gene transcription is tightly regulated according to growth conditions through the stress-sensitive transcription factor Ifh1.
source: In S. cerevisiae, RP gene transcription is known to be tightly regulated according to growth conditions through the stress-sensitive transcription factor (TF) Ifh1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast RP gene regulation.

claim: Ifh1 is rapidly released from RP promoters only minutes following inhibition of TORC1 kinase.
source: Thus, Ifh1 is rapidly released from RP promoters only minutes following inhibition of the conserved eukaryotic growth regulator Target Of Rapamycin Complex 1 (TORC1) kinase (Schawalder et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schawalder et al., 2004.

claim: Ifh1 promoter binding is coordinated with RNA polymerase I (RNAPI) activity upon prolonged TORC1 inhibition to help balance RP and rRNA production.
source: Although it has been shown that Ifh1 promoter binding is coordinated with RNA polymerase I (RNAPI) activity upon prolonged TORC1 inhibition to help balance RP and rRNA production (Albert et al., 2016; Rudra et al., 2007), how Ifh1 is removed from RP gene promoters to immediately downregulate their expression following stress remains a mystery.
evidence: Supported by citations to Albert et al., 2016; Rudra et al., 2007.

claim: Top1 depletion triggers rapid repression of RP genes and activation of proteostasis genes.
source: However, Top1 depletion triggered a rapid response at two specific groups of genes: upregulation of Hsf1 target genes and downregulation of RP genes (Figure 1A,D; Figure 1—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,D and supplementary figures.

claim: The transcriptional response to Top1 depletion is transient, with both RP and Hsf1 target genes returning to normal levels by 60 min.
source: Remarkably, this response was transient, as both groups of genes returned to normal levels (i.e. before auxin addition) by 60 min.
evidence: Based on experimental observations described in the text.

claim: Re-equilibration of gene expression following Top1 depletion is dependent upon Top2.
source: This re-equilibration was dependent upon Top2 since it failed to occur in the Top1/2-AID strain, where prolonged auxin treatment led to significant dysregulation of many other RNAPII-transcribed genes (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Top1 depletion triggers a highly specific stress response linked to RP genes and Hsf1 target genes.
source: This analysis shows clearly that Top1 depletion, as well as depletion of both Top1 and Top2 (at the early 20 min time point), triggers a highly specific stress response linked to RP genes and Hsf1 target genes (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-C.

claim: The activator Ifh1 is rapidly released from RP gene promoters after topoisomerases depletion.
source: Interestingly, we found that the activator Ifh1 is rapidly released from RP gene promoters after topoisomerases depletion (Figure 1E), whereas Rap1 and Fhl1, which bind directly to RP promoter DNA, are not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and supplementary figures.

claim: Rap1 and Fhl1 binding to RP promoters is not affected by topoisomerase depletion.
source: whereas Rap1 and Fhl1, which bind directly to RP promoter DNA, are not affected (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Hsf1 nuclear depletion completely abolishes activation of stress genes following Top1 depletion without affecting down-regulation of RP genes.
source: This experiment revealed that Hsf1 nuclear depletion completely abolishes activation of stress genes following Top1 depletion without affecting down-regulation of RP genes (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Activation of stress-induced genes following Top1 depletion is completely Hsf1-dependent.
source: Therefore, activation of stress-induced genes following Top1 depletion is completely Hsf1-dependent, whereas repression of RP genes is independent of Hsf1 or the induction of its target genes.
evidence: Based on experimental results with Hsf1 depletion.

claim: Repression of RP genes following Top1 depletion is independent of Hsf1 or the induction of its target genes.
source: Therefore, activation of stress-induced genes following Top1 depletion is completely Hsf1-dependent, whereas repression of RP genes is independent of Hsf1 or the induction of its target genes.
evidence: Based on experimental results with Hsf1 depletion.

claim: Top1 depletion causes formation of distinct nuclear foci by the Btn2 aggregase.
source: Although it may seem surprising that depletion of topoisomerases can induce a Hsf1-dependent stress response, formation of distinct nuclear foci by the Btn2 aggregase and perinuclear accumulation of the proteasome subunit Pre6 following Top1/2 degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) both point to the induction of proteotoxic stress in the nucleus (Miller et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and citation to Miller et al., 2015a.

claim: Top1 depletion causes perinuclear accumulation of the proteasome subunit Pre6.
source: Although it may seem surprising that depletion of topoisomerases can induce a Hsf1-dependent stress response, formation of distinct nuclear foci by the Btn2 aggregase and perinuclear accumulation of the proteasome subunit Pre6 following Top1/2 degradation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B) both point to the induction of proteotoxic stress in the nucleus (Miller et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and citation to Miller et al., 2015a.

claim: Top1 was initially identified through a mutation (mak1) defective in large ribosomal subunit production.
source: Top1 was initially identified through a mutation (mak1) defective in large ribosomal subunit production (Thrash et al., 1985) and was later shown to be required for proper rRNA synthesis (Brill et al., 1987; El Hage et al., 2010; French et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Thrash et al., 1985; Brill et al., 1987; El Hage et al., 2010; French et al., 2011.

claim: Top1 is required for proper rRNA synthesis.
source: and was later shown to be required for proper rRNA synthesis (Brill et al., 1987; El Hage et al., 2010; French et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brill et al., 1987; El Hage et al., 2010; French et al., 2011.

claim: Top1 depletion causes a strong reduction of pre-rRNA synthesis as early as 10 min after auxin addition.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed a strong reduction of pre-rRNA synthesis as shown by decreased [3H]-adenine pulse-labeling of the RNAPI-transcribed 35S pre-rRNA, and two co-transcriptionally cleaved products, 27S and 20S pre-rRNAs, as early as 10 min after initiation of Top1 (or Top1 and Top2) depletion by addition of auxin to the medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Top1 depletion causes an elongation defect in rRNA synthesis, shown by accumulation of truncated pre-rRNAs.
source: This decreased rRNA synthesis is accompanied by an elongation defect, as shown by the accumulation of truncated pre-rRNAs that were initially described by the Tollervey laboratory (El Hage et al., 2010; Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and citation to El Hage et al., 2010.

claim: Top1 depletion leads to unbalanced production of 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, with a marked deficiency of the large (60S) subunit relative to the small (40S) subunit.
source: Further downstream, the rapid defect in rRNA production caused by inhibition of RNAPI elongation leads to unbalanced production of 40S and 60S ribosomal subunits, with a marked deficiency of the large (60S) subunit relative to the small (40S) subunit (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Following topoisomerase degradation, both large and small subunit proteins (Rpl3 and Rps8) accumulate in trailing fractions of polysome gradients.
source: Consistent with this, we detect accumulation of both and large and small subunit proteins (Rpl3 and Rps8, respectively) in trailing fractions of polysome gradients (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: RPs fail to be incorporated normally into ribosomes immediately following topoisomerase degradation.
source: These observations strongly suggest that RPs fail to be incorporated normally into ribosomes immediately following topoisomerase degradation.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental observations.

claim: Newly synthetized, unassembled RPs accumulate in aggregates in response to ribosome assembly stress.
source: RPs are known to be prone to aggregation (David et al., 2010; Pillet et al., 2017; Rand and Grant, 2006; Weids et al., 2016) and recent reports show that newly synthetized, unassembled RPs accumulate in aggregates in response to ribosome assembly stress (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: RPs accumulate in an insoluble fraction following topoisomerase degradation.
source: Significantly, we also observed accumulation of RPs in an insoluble fraction following topoisomerase degradation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Depletion of Utp8 triggers a similar transcriptional response to Top1 depletion, namely downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Remarkably, all these treatments triggered a similar transcriptional response to that which occurs following Top1 depletion, namely a specific downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes (Figure 2E–G; Supplementary file 2), which we refer to as the 'Ribosome Assembly STress Response' (RASTR).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Depletion of Utp13 triggers a similar transcriptional response to Top1 depletion, namely downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Remarkably, all these treatments triggered a similar transcriptional response to that which occurs following Top1 depletion, namely a specific downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes (Figure 2E–G; Supplementary file 2), which we refer to as the 'Ribosome Assembly STress Response' (RASTR).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Diazaborine treatment triggers a similar transcriptional response to Top1 depletion, namely downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Remarkably, all these treatments triggered a similar transcriptional response to that which occurs following Top1 depletion, namely a specific downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes (Figure 2E–G; Supplementary file 2), which we refer to as the 'Ribosome Assembly STress Response' (RASTR).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-G.

claim: Utp8 is a member of the t-UTP subcomplex of 90S pre-ribosomes.
source: Utp8p is a member of the t-UTP subcomplex of 90S pre-ribosomes and its depletion inhibits rDNA transcription, leading to a reduction of the primary 35S pre-rRNA transcript and subsequent processing intermediates (Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallagher et al., 2004.

claim: Utp8 depletion inhibits rDNA transcription, leading to a reduction of the primary 35S pre-rRNA transcript and subsequent processing intermediates.
source: Utp8p is a member of the t-UTP subcomplex of 90S pre-ribosomes and its depletion inhibits rDNA transcription, leading to a reduction of the primary 35S pre-rRNA transcript and subsequent processing intermediates (Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallagher et al., 2004.

claim: Utp13 is a member of the UTP-B subcomplex.
source: In contrast, depletion of Utp13 (a member of the UTP-B subcomplex) interferes with downstream processing and synthesis of 40S subunits and causes decreased 18S rRNA levels without affecting the levels of the 25S or 5.8S rRNAs (Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallagher et al., 2004.

claim: Utp13 depletion interferes with downstream processing and synthesis of 40S subunits and causes decreased 18S rRNA levels without affecting the levels of the 25S or 5.8S rRNAs.
source: In contrast, depletion of Utp13 (a member of the UTP-B subcomplex) interferes with downstream processing and synthesis of 40S subunits and causes decreased 18S rRNA levels without affecting the levels of the 25S or 5.8S rRNAs (Gallagher et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gallagher et al., 2004.

claim: Diazaborine is an inhibitor of the essential Drg1 AAA-ATPase that rapidly blocks mid-late steps of 60S subunit maturation.
source: Diazaborine, an inhibitor of the essential Drg1 AAA-ATPase, rapidly blocks mid-late steps of 60S subunit maturation (Loibl et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Loibl et al., 2014.

claim: The RQC binds to 60S ribosomal subunits containing stalled polypeptides and leads to their degradation.
source: A pioneering study reported that a set of proteins termed the RQC binds to 60S ribosomal subunits containing stalled polypeptides and leads to their degradation.
evidence: Refers to a pioneering study, implicitly citing previous work.

claim: The RQC triggers a specific stress signal that leads to Hsf1 target gene activation.
source: In the process, the RQC triggers a specific stress signal that leads to Hsf1 target gene activation (Brandman et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: Cells lacking Tae2 fail to activate Hsf1 following translational stress.
source: Thus, cells lacking a component of the RQC, the Tae2 protein, fail to activate Hsf1 following translational stress.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the RQC pathway.

claim: Activation of Hsf1 target genes and downregulation of RP genes following Top1/2 depletion is unaffected by deletion of TAE2.
source: We found that activation of two Hsf1 target genes (SSA1 and HSP42) and downregulation of two RP genes (RPL30 and RPL39) was unaffected by deletion of TAE2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) and conclude that RQC does not play a role in RASTR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: RQC does not play a role in RASTR.
source: and conclude that RQC does not play a role in RASTR.
evidence: Based on experimental results with tae2 deletion.

claim: Cells have developed distinct mechanisms to adapt the Hsf1 transcriptional program to defects in both ribosome activity and ribosome assembly.
source: These results highlight that cells have developed distinct mechanisms to adapt the Hsf1 transcriptional program to defects in both ribosome activity and ribosome assembly.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results.

claim: Ifh1 association with RP gene promoters in growing cells is rapidly disrupted (within 5 min) following inhibition of TORC1 kinase by rapamycin.
source: We reported previously that the association of Ifh1 with RP gene promoters in growing cells is rapidly disrupted (within 5 min) following inhibition of the growth-promoting TORC1 kinase by addition of rapamycin to the medium (Schawalder et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schawalder et al., 2004.

claim: Stable release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters (measured 20 min after rapamycin addition) requires its C-terminal domain together with a complex of proteins containing casein kinase 2 (CK2) and two RiBi factors, Utp22 and Rrp7.
source: More recently (Albert et al., 2016), we found that stable release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters (measured 20 min after rapamycin addition) requires its C-terminal domain together with a complex of proteins containing casein kinase 2 (CK2) and two RiBi factors, Utp22 and Rrp7, with which Ifh1 interacts to form the CURI complex (Rudra et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Albert et al., 2016 and Rudra et al., 2007.

claim: In ifh1-ΔC cells, the truncated protein is rapidly released but later returns to RP gene promoters following TORC1 inhibition.
source: Thus, in ifh1-ΔC cells the truncated protein is rapidly released but later returns to RP gene promoters following TORC1 inhibition.
evidence: Based on previous experimental observations.

claim: ifh1-ΔC promoter release is stable following Top1 depletion.
source: Interestingly, ifh1-ΔC promoter release is stable following Top1 depletion, suggesting that an unknown mechanism regulates Ifh1 during RASTR (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: RP gene repression and Hsf1 target gene activation occur with identical kinetics following RASTR activation.
source: The fact that RP gene repression and Hsf1 target gene activation occur with identical kinetics following RASTR activation (Figure 3B), and that Ifh1 concentrates in nuclear foci rapidly after topoisomerase depletion (Figure 3C), suggests that Ifh1 could be sensitive to the accumulation of unassembled RPs in the nucleus, as is presumably the case for Hsf1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Ifh1 concentrates in nuclear foci rapidly after topoisomerase depletion.
source: The fact that RP gene repression and Hsf1 target gene activation occur with identical kinetics following RASTR activation (Figure 3B), and that Ifh1 concentrates in nuclear foci rapidly after topoisomerase depletion (Figure 3C), suggests that Ifh1 could be sensitive to the accumulation of unassembled RPs in the nucleus, as is presumably the case for Hsf1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In cells lacking Tom1, Ifh1 accumulates in prominent nuclear foci even in the absence of stress.
source: To begin with, in cells lacking Tom1, an E3 ligase required for degradation of unassembled RPs (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b), but not in TOM1 cells, Ifh1 accumulates in prominent nuclear foci even in the absence of stress (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and citations.

claim: Tom1 is an E3 ligase required for degradation of unassembled RPs.
source: To begin with, in cells lacking Tom1, an E3 ligase required for degradation of unassembled RPs (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b), but not in TOM1 cells, Ifh1 accumulates in prominent nuclear foci even in the absence of stress (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b.

claim: tom1-Δ is synthetically lethal with ifh1-AA.
source: Remarkably, tom1-Δ is synthetically lethal with ifh1-AA (Figure 3E) supporting the notion that RP aggregation could directly impact on Ifh1 promoter binding.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: tom1-Δ is not synthetically lethal with ifh1-6.
source: Remarkably, tom1-Δ is not synthetically lethal with ifh1-6 (Figure 3E), supporting the notion that genetic interaction with ifh1-AA is directly linked to the ability of Ifh1 to bind RP gene promoters.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The insoluble fraction following topoisomerase depletion is enriched in chaperones and RPs.
source: As previously reported for tom1-Δ cells (Sung et al., 2016a), the insoluble fraction is enriched in chaperones and RPs (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G and citation.

claim: Following topoisomerase depletion, there is a strong increase in RiBi factors in the insoluble fraction, primarily those implicated in biogenesis of the large ribosomal subunit.
source: We also noted a strong increase in RiBi factors, primarily those implicated in biogenesis of the large ribosomal subunit (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Ifh1 was never detected in an insoluble fraction in the absence of stress but was invariably detected in these fractions following topoisomerase depletion.
source: Importantly, Ifh1 was never detected in an insoluble fraction in the absence of stress but was invariably detected in these fractions following topoisomerase depletion (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in supplementary file.

claim: Ifh1 binding is highly specific to RP genes.
source: It is important to note that Ifh1 binding is highly specific to RP genes (Knight et al., 2014) and that the transcriptional effect of its nuclear depletion is restricted to RP genes and a very small number of additional targets (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by citation to Knight et al., 2014 and experimental data in supplementary file.

claim: Ifh1 depletion by anchor-away leads to a significant and highly specific decrease in RP gene transcription.
source: it nonetheless leads to a significant and highly specific decrease in RP gene transcription as measured by RNAPII ChIP-seq (Figure 4B; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ifh1 depletion leads to aberrant rRNA processing.
source: Interestingly, Ifh1 depletion also leads to aberrant rRNA processing (Figure 4C) as would expected in conditions where RP levels become limiting (Reiter et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and citation to Reiter et al., 2011.

claim: 60 min of Ifh1 anchoring alone causes a significant down-regulation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Remarkably, we noted that 60 min of Ifh1 anchoring alone, in the absence of topoisomerase depletion, also caused a significant down-regulation of Hsf1 target genes (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 4) even though Ifh1 is absent from the promoters of these genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the Hsf1 transcriptional program is continuously influenced by RP production.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures.

claim: Upregulation of Hsf1 target genes was either abolished or strongly reduced when Top1 or Top1 and Top2 were degraded following nuclear depletion of Ifh1.
source: Consistent with this idea, we found that upregulation of Hsf1 target genes was either abolished or strongly reduced (Figure 4E,F,G; Supplementary file 4) when Top1 or Top1 and Top2 were degraded following nuclear depletion of Ifh1, indicating that RP production is required for Hsf1 target gene activation during RASTR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E,F,G.

claim: RP production is required for Hsf1 target gene activation during RASTR.
source: indicating that RP production is required for Hsf1 target gene activation during RASTR.
evidence: Based on experimental results with Ifh1 depletion.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment blocks all translational elongations, leading to rapid depletion of the nuclear pools of RPs.
source: As an alternative approach to test the requirement for de novo RP synthesis to initiate RASTR we used cycloheximide treatment, which blocks all translational elongations, thus leading to rapid depletion of the nuclear pools of RPs (Figure 5A; Gorenstein and Warner, 1977; Warner, 1977; Reiter et al., 2011; Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cycloheximide alone triggers a rapid arrest of rRNA processing.
source: As reported by others (Reiter et al., 2011), we confirmed that cycloheximide alone also triggers a rapid arrest of rRNA processing (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and citation to Reiter et al., 2011.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment triggers a transcriptional response exactly opposite to that induced by RASTR, namely Hsf1 target gene downregulation and RP gene upregulation.
source: Quite strikingly, we observed a transcriptional response to cycloheximide treatment exactly opposite to that induced by RASTR, namely Hsf1 target gene downregulation and RP gene upregulation (Figure 5C; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Even in unstressed cells RP production may contribute to a basal level of Hsf1 activation while at the same time limiting Ifh1 activity at RP gene promoters.
source: This finding suggests that even in unstressed cells RP production may contribute to a basal level of Hsf1 activation while at the same time limiting Ifh1 activity at RP gene promoters.
evidence: Based on inference from cycloheximide experiments.

claim: Treatment of cells undergoing Top1 or Top1/2 depletion with cycloheximide completely abolished both RP gene repression and activation of Hsf1 target genes.
source: Significantly, treatment of cells undergoing Top1 or Top1/2 depletion with cycloheximide (auxin + CHX) completely abolished both RP gene repression and activation of Hsf1 target genes (Figure 5D,E; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: RASTR is dependent upon de novo protein synthesis.
source: These findings clearly demonstrate that RASTR is dependent upon de novo protein synthesis.
evidence: Based on experimental results with cycloheximide.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment efficiently prevents aggregation of newly synthesized RPs following proteasome inhibition.
source: Importantly, it was recently reported that cycloheximide treatment efficiently prevents aggregation of newly synthesized RPs following proteasome inhibition (Sung et al., 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sung et al., 2016a.

claim: CHX treatment leads to strong reduction of Ifh1-eGFP nuclear foci that are observed in cells lacking Tom1.
source: Perhaps as a direct consequence of this, we found that CHX treatment also leads to strong reduction of Ifh1-eGFP nuclear foci that are observed in cells lacking the ubiquitin ligase Tom1, which is specifically required for efficient degradation of unassembled RPs (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b; Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure and citations.

claim: Ifh1 dis-aggregation following cycloheximide exposure is associated with increased Ifh1 binding at a RP gene promoter, which becomes significant in tom1-Δ cells.
source: Furthermore, Ifh1 dis-aggregation following cycloheximide exposure is associated with increased Ifh1 binding at a RP gene promoter, which becomes significant in tom1-Δ cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment prevents the release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters in response to the activation of RASTR by topoisomerase depletion.
source: Similarly, cycloheximide treatment also prevents the release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters in response to the activation of RASTR by topoisomerase depletion (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figure.

claim: There is a large increase in cells that accumulate RP (Rpl25) or Ifh1 nuclear aggregates during RASTR that is abolished in the presence of cycloheximide.
source: Consistent with this view, we observed a large increase in cells that accumulate RP (Rpl25) or Ifh1 nuclear aggregates during RASTR that is abolished in the presence of cycloheximide (Figure 5F,G; Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F,G and supplementary figures.

claim: Newly synthetized RPs, in both stressed and unstressed cells, operate as a central hub in coordinating the expression of RP genes themselves with the Hsf1-dependent activation of chaperone and proteasome genes.
source: More generally, these data indicate that newly synthetized RPs, in both stressed and unstressed cells, operate as a central hub in coordinating the expression of RP genes themselves with the Hsf1-dependent activation of chaperone and proteasome genes.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: Rapamycin triggers a rapid arrest of rRNA processing.
source: As reported previously, rapamycin triggers a rapid arrest of rRNA processing (Figure 6A) and a decrease of RP and RiBi gene expression (Figure 6B,C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Rapamycin causes a decrease of RP and RiBi gene expression.
source: As reported previously, rapamycin triggers a rapid arrest of rRNA processing (Figure 6A) and a decrease of RP and RiBi gene expression (Figure 6B,C; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: Hsf1 target genes are transiently up- and downregulated at 5 and 20 min, respectively, following rapamycin addition.
source: Interestingly, we noted that Hsf1 target genes are transiently up- and downregulated at 5 and 20 min, respectively, following rapamycin addition (Figure 6B,C; Supplementary file 6), suggesting that RASTR is activated at the early time point but shortly thereafter turned off.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,C.

claim: RP production ceases around 15 min after rapamycin treatment.
source: Consistent with this view, it has been reported that RP production ceases around 15 min after rapamycin treatment (Reiter et al., 2011), which we suggest would turn off the signal for RASTR, thus explaining the downregulation of Hsf1 target genes observed at 20 min.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reiter et al., 2011.

claim: Cycloheximide pre-treatment specifically prevented RP gene repression and Hsf1 target gene activation at 5 min following rapamycin addition.
source: Remarkably, this specifically prevented RP gene repression and Hsf1 target gene activation at 5 min following rapamycin addition, whereas at the longer time point (20 min) RP genes and Hsf1 were regulated independently of cycloheximide (Figure 6D,E; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Cycloheximide pre-treatment prevents release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters at 5 min, but not at 20 min following rapamycin treatment.
source: Consistent with the early block in RP gene downregulation being due to a failure to initiate RASTR immediately following rapamycin addition, we showed that cycloheximide pre-treatment prevents release of Ifh1 from RP gene promoters at 5 min, but not at 20 min following rapamycin treatment (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Regulation of RP gene transcription following TORC1 inactivation by rapamycin operates through two distinct mechanisms at short and long timescales.
source: The effects of rapamycin treatment described above are fully consistent with our previous report demonstrating that regulation of RP gene transcription following TORC1 inactivation by rapamycin operates through two distinct mechanisms at short and long timescales, with the latter dependent on RNAPI activity and the CURI complex (Albert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Albert et al., 2016.

claim: Heat shock causes strong downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes only 5 min following a shift in temperature to 40°C.
source: As expected, we observed strong downregulation of RP genes and upregulation of Hsf1 target genes only 5 min following a shift in temperature to 40°C (Figure 7A–C, left panels) that was also accompanied by strong upregulation of Msn2 target genes and downregulation of RiBi genes (Figure 7A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: Cycloheximide pre-treatment prevents the strong and immediate repression of RP genes following heat shock.
source: Remarkably, though, we found that cycloheximide pre-treatment prevents the strong and immediate repression of RP genes following heat shock (Figure 7A,B; right panels; Supplementary file 6), consistent again with the idea that this facet of the heat-shock response is identical to that which occurs during RASTR.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: Hsf1 target genes are still activated following heat shock in the presence of cycloheximide.
source: Importantly though, Hsf1 target genes are still activated following heat shock in the presence of cycloheximide (Figure 7A,C; right panels), presumably because the unfolding of thermo-labile proteins induced by heat shock is alone sufficient to activate Hsf1 even in the absence of continuing RP synthesis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,C.

claim: RASTR may constitute the earliest transcriptional response, at the level of RNAPII, to a wide variety of stress conditions.
source: Nevertheless, the striking requirement for de novo protein synthesis for RP gene downregulation following heat shock strongly suggests that RASTR plays an integral role in this component of the heat-shock response and thus may constitute the earliest transcriptional response, at the level of RNAPII, to a wide variety of stress conditions.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental results with heat shock and cycloheximide.

claim: RASTR is a novel regulatory pathway that allows rapid and simultaneous up-regulation of protein homeostasis genes and downregulation of RP genes following disruption of various steps in ribosome biogenesis.
source: In this study, we uncover a novel regulatory pathway, hereafter referred to as the Ribosomal Assembly Stress Response (RASTR), that allows rapid and simultaneous up-regulation of protein homeostasis genes and downregulation of RP genes following disruption of various steps in ribosome biogenesis (rRNA production, processing or RP assembly).
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main findings.

claim: RASTR is highly specific to the RP and Hsf1 regulons, with little or no effect on a much larger group of genes implicated in the Environmental Stress Response (ESR).
source: We show that RASTR is highly specific to the RP and Hsf1 regulons, with little or no effect on a much larger group of genes implicated in the Environmental Stress Response (ESR).
evidence: Based on experimental data comparing different gene groups.

claim: RASTR requires neo-synthesis of RPs following stress.
source: Importantly, RASTR requires neo-synthesis of RPs following stress and is linked to the accumulation of RP aggregates, which we propose lead to Hsf1 activation, through chaperone competition, and to the sequestration of Ifh1 in an insoluble nucleolar fraction.
evidence: Based on experimental results with Ifh1 depletion and cycloheximide.

claim: RASTR is linked to the accumulation of RP aggregates.
source: Importantly, RASTR requires neo-synthesis of RPs following stress and is linked to the accumulation of RP aggregates, which we propose lead to Hsf1 activation, through chaperone competition, and to the sequestration of Ifh1 in an insoluble nucleolar fraction.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing RP accumulation in insoluble fractions.

claim: RP aggregates lead to Hsf1 activation through chaperone competition.
source: which we propose lead to Hsf1 activation, through chaperone competition, and to the sequestration of Ifh1 in an insoluble nucleolar fraction.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: RP aggregates lead to the sequestration of Ifh1 in an insoluble nucleolar fraction.
source: which we propose lead to Hsf1 activation, through chaperone competition, and to the sequestration of Ifh1 in an insoluble nucleolar fraction.
evidence: Based on experimental data showing Ifh1 in insoluble fractions.

claim: Protein synthesis inhabitation via cycloheximide treatment leads to a transcriptional response opposite to that of RASTR.
source: Notably, we show that protein synthesis inhabitation via cycloheximide treatment leads to a transcriptional response opposite to that of RASTR, supporting a model in which unstressed cells constantly monitor nuclear levels of unassembled RPs and use this information to balance expression of Hsf1 target genes with those encoding RPs.
evidence: Based on experimental data with cycloheximide.

claim: Unstressed cells constantly monitor nuclear levels of unassembled RPs and use this information to balance expression of Hsf1 target genes with those encoding RPs.
source: supporting a model in which unstressed cells constantly monitor nuclear levels of unassembled RPs and use this information to balance expression of Hsf1 target genes with those encoding RPs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental observations.

claim: RASTR is the initial transcriptional response to inactivation of TORC1 kinase.
source: Finally, we demonstrate that RASTR is the initial transcriptional response to inactivation of TORC1 kinase, supporting a key role for this regulatory pathway in the activation of a protein homeostasis transcriptional program that allows cells to cope with the proteotoxic consequences of disruptions to ribosome biogenesis.
evidence: Based on experimental data with rapamycin treatment.

claim: Disequilibrium at any step-in ribosome biogenesis will lead to RASTR activation until the pool of unassembled RPs decreases.
source: Our data indicate that disequilibrium at any step-in ribosome biogenesis (rRNA transcription, early or late rRNA processing or assembly) will lead to RASTR activation until the pool of unassembled RPs decreases.
evidence: Based on experimental results with different perturbations to ribosome biogenesis.

claim: RPs are among the most abundant ubiquitinylated proteins that accumulate in the nucleus of proteasome-deficient S. cerevisiae and human cells.
source: It is important to note that RPs are among the most abundant ubiquitinylated proteins that accumulate in the nucleus of proteasome-deficient S. cerevisiae and human cells (Sung et al., 2016a; Sung et al., 2016b; Lam et al., 2007; Mayor et al., 2007), suggesting that the synthesis of RPs and their assembly into ribosomes must be tightly coordinated with the cell's proteostasis capacity.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations.

claim: Induction of ribosome assembly stress is correlated with the rapid accumulation of RPs in a detergent-insoluble fraction.
source: Consistent with this view, we show here that induction of ribosome assembly stress is correlated with the rapid accumulation of RPs in a detergent-insoluble fraction and that blocking de novo RP production, either by anchoring away Ifh1 or treating cells with cycloheximide, diminishes or abolishes a key transcriptional consequence of RASTR, namely upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
evidence: Based on experimental data.

claim: Blocking de novo RP production diminishes or abolishes upregulation of Hsf1 target genes during RASTR.
source: and that blocking de novo RP production, either by anchoring away Ifh1 or treating cells with cycloheximide, diminishes or abolishes a key transcriptional consequence of RASTR, namely upregulation of Hsf1 target genes.
evidence: Based on experimental data with Ifh1 depletion and cycloheximide.

claim: RP aggregates are an important activating signal for RASTR.
source: Our observations thus strongly suggest that RP aggregates are an important activating signal for RASTR.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple experimental results.

claim: A large number of additional proteins accumulate in an insoluble fraction upon ribosome assembly stress, including many RiBi proteins, the RP gene activator Ifh1, and chaperones.
source: Nevertheless, we and others (Sung et al., 2016a) detect a large number of additional proteins that accumulate in an insoluble fraction upon ribosome assembly stress, including many RiBi proteins (e.g. numerous rRNA helicases and processing factors), the RP gene activator Ifh1, and chaperones.
evidence: Based on experimental data and citation.

claim: RP- and Ifh1-containing aggregates are highly dynamic.
source: In any event, our data suggest that RP- and Ifh1-containing aggregates are highly dynamic since the promoter release of Ifh1 and activation of Hsf1 following Top1 degradation are rapidly reversed by Top2 compensation (Figure 1) and Ifh1 aggregates that appear in tom1-Δ cells quickly diminish following cycloheximide treatment (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on experimental observations.

claim: Nucleolar proteins can form sub-compartmental structures by promoting liquid-liquid phase separation.
source: Interestingly, it has recently been reported that nucleolar proteins can form sub-compartmental structures by promoting liquid-liquid phase separation (Berry et al., 2015; Feric et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Berry et al., 2015; Feric et al., 2016.

claim: In strains where RNAPI is constitutively active, Ifh1 is released from RP gene promoters shortly after TORC1 inhibition by rapamycin treatment (~5 min) but returns only 15 min later.
source: We showed previously (Albert et al., 2016) that in strains where RNAPI is constitutively active (Laferté et al., 2006) Ifh1 is released from RP gene promoters shortly after TORC1 inhibition by rapamycin treatment (~5 min) but returns only 15 min later.
evidence: Supported by citations to Albert et al., 2016 and Laferté et al., 2006.

claim: Two RiBi proteins (Utp22 and Rrp7) can sequester Ifh1 in the CURI complex.
source: This promoter re-binding does not occur in wild-type cells due to the action of two RiBi proteins (Utp22 and Rrp7) that can sequester Ifh1 in the CURI (Casein Kinase 2/Utp22/Rrp7/Ifh1) complex (Albert et al., 2016; Rudra et al., 2007) allowing to re-align RP gene expression with RNAPI activity.
evidence: Supported by citations to Albert et al., 2016; Rudra et al., 2007.

claim: S. cerevisiae has developed temporally distinct mechanisms to regulate RP gene expression.
source: These findings revealed that S. cerevisiae has developed temporally distinct mechanisms to regulate RP gene expression.
evidence: Based on previous findings cited in the text.

claim: The short timescale mechanism of RP gene regulation results from a rapid rise in unassembled RPs that occurs immediately following TORC1 inhibition, or other stresses that disrupt ribosome assembly.
source: One of the keys finding in the present study is to confirm the existence of a two-step process in RP gene regulation and to link the first step to control of the Hsf1 regulon. We propose that this short timescale mechanism results from a rapid rise in unassembled RPs that occurs immediately following TORC1 inhibition, or other stresses that disrupt ribosome assembly, such as depletion of Top1 or RiBi factors.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental findings.

claim: The rapid induction of Hsf1 target genes, in combination with the arrest of RP gene transcription, contributes to the eventual clearing of proteotoxic unassembled RPs from the nucleus.
source: Following ribosome assembly stress, we imagine that the rapid induction of Hsf1 target genes, in combination with the arrest of RP gene transcription, contributes to the eventual clearing of proteotoxic unassembled RPs from the nucleus, thereby removing the signal that promotes RASTR and leads to Ifh1 promoter release and Hsf1 activation.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on experimental observations.

claim: Ribosome assembly stress in higher eukaryotes has been studied extensively in the context of ribosomopathies.
source: As alluded to above, ribosome assembly stress in higher eukaryotes has been studied extensively in the context of ribosomopathies, diseases often associated with RP gene haplo-insufficiencies, RP gene point mutations or mutations in RiBi factors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ribosomopathies.

claim: Unassembled RPs trigger a feedback mechanism that decreases transcription of ribosome biogenesis genes by inhibiting c-Myc function and arrests cell growth through p53 activation.
source: One hypothesis put forward to explain these observations is that unassembled RPs trigger a feedback mechanism that decreases transcription of ribosome biogenesis genes by inhibiting c-Myc function and arrests cell growth through p53 activation (Dai et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dai et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2016.

claim: The rRNA helicase DDX21 binds to and activates RP gene promoters in a manner that may be sensitive to the status of ribosome biogenesis.
source: It has also been recently reported that the rRNA helicase DDX21 binds to and activates RP gene promoters in a manner that may be sensitive to the status of ribosome biogenesis (Calo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calo et al., 2015.

claim: Unassembled RPs could mediate an ancestral process to regulate ribosome biogenesis conserved from prokaryotes to eukaryotes.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that unassembled RPs could mediate an ancestral process to regulate ribosome biogenesis conserved from prokaryotes (Nomura, 1999) to eukaryotes.
evidence: Based on inference from multiple findings and citation to Nomura, 1999.

claim: Hsf1 is a key sensor of proteotoxic stress in all eukaryotes that controls a common set of chaperones conserved from yeast to human.
source: Hsf1 is a key sensor of proteotoxic stress in all eukaryotes that controls a common set of chaperones conserved from yeast to human.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hsf1.

claim: Hsf1 reduces protein aggregate formation leading to neurogenerative diseases.
source: One protective function reported for Hsf1 is its ability to reduce protein aggregate formation leading to neurogenerative diseases (Neef et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Neef et al., 2014.

claim: Hsf1 exerts a pro-oncogenic function through its ability to promote proteostasis in rapidly growing tumor cells.
source: On the other hand, Hsf1 also exerts a pro-oncogenic function through its ability to promote proteostasis in rapidly growing tumor cells (Mendillo et al., 2012; Santagata et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mendillo et al., 2012; Santagata et al., 2011.

claim: Hsf1 activity is tightly linked to ribosome biogenesis in yeast, in a manner independent of the RQC mechanism.
source: Our work and that of Tye et al. (2018) demonstrates that Hsf1 activity is tightly linked to ribosome biogenesis in yeast, in a manner independent of the previously described RQC mechanism that contributes to the dissociation of aberrant nascent polypeptides from the ribosome (Brandman et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on experimental findings from this study and citation to Tye et al., 2018 and Brandman et al., 2012.

claim: RPs are subjected to a high turnover rate compared to other nuclear components in mammalian cells.
source: Although it is currently unknown if RASTR is conserved in metazoans, we note that RPs are also subjected to a high turnover rate compared to other nuclear components in mammalian cells and that proteasome or ribosome assembly inhibition trigger a rapid accumulation of RPs in the nucleus, whereas arrest of translation has an opposite effect (Sung et al., 2016a; Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a; Lam et al., 2007.

claim: Proteasome or ribosome assembly inhibition trigger a rapid accumulation of RPs in the nucleus in mammalian cells, whereas arrest of translation has an opposite effect.
source: and that proteasome or ribosome assembly inhibition trigger a rapid accumulation of RPs in the nucleus, whereas arrest of translation has an opposite effect (Sung et al., 2016a; Lam et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sung et al., 2016a; Lam et al., 2007.

claim: Cycloheximide treatment abolishes Hsf1 activity in mammalian cells by an unknown mechanism.
source: Importantly, it was reported that cycloheximide treatment also abolishes Hsf1 activity in mammalian cell by an unknown mechanism (Santagata et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Santagata et al., 2013.

claim: A dynamic balance between unassembled and assembled RPs could be sensed by Hsf1 to constantly adjust protein homeostasis transcription programs in eukaryotes with translational flux, proteolysis and the rate of ribosome assembly.
source: We propose that a dynamic balance between unassembled and assembled RPs could be sensed by Hsf1 to constantly adjust protein homeostasis transcription programs in eukaryotes with translational flux, proteolysis and the rate of ribosome assembly (Figure 8), since disruption or hyperactivation of any of these processes will rapidly change nuclear levels of free RPs.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental findings.
